Key data: the state currently has room under the SAL ($27B in 2026-27 per LAO/administration estimates). But if revenue grows (e.g., AI boom, capital gains), the state could hit the limit — meaning Prop 41's Section 3 could force rebates/school spending instead of program spending, and could effectively block spending of new dedicated tax revenue (e.g., a transportation tax, a health care tax) when the state is at the limit. Also LWV notes Prop 41 would apply to programs such as public campaign financing that may not receive General Fund support.

Also there's an important technical issue: the Gann Limit's exclusion mechanism — under Article XIII B, certain revenues are excluded ("proceeds of taxes" definitions exclude things like federal funds, bond proceeds, etc.), and the Legislature can adjust the limit by statute under Section 4 (as Prop 35 did for MCO tax). Prop 41's Section 4(b)(2) prohibits that mechanism for new taxes. This would create a genuine problem for provider taxes (MCO tax, hospital fee, SNF fee) which leverage federal matching funds — those rely on the appropriations limit adjustment. That's a real fiscal risk of billions of dollars in federal Medi-Cal matching funds.

Let me verify this point independently — is there an LAO or nonpartisan source noting Prop 41's potential effect on MCO tax/provider taxes? The CalBudgetCenter brief mentioned: "some health care financing sources that must be occasionally reauthorized — such as the Managed Care Organization (MCO) tax and the Hospital Quality Assurance fee... could potentially be impacted by Prop. 41. This, in turn, would jeopardize billions of dollars in federal funding for Medi-Cal."

Good — that's a nonpartisan analysis from the California Budget & Policy Center, corroborating the Berkeley memo.

One more important angle: the audit requirement's practicality. The State Auditor would have to audit every special tax initiative at the 25% signature stage — including frivolous ones. There could be many. The LAO estimates low millions per year. Also, the auditor is required to audit "each program that would receive moneys" — for a brand-new program, there's nothing to audit yet, so it would be auditing the existing analogous program (e.g., for the billionaire tax, Medi-Cal). For Prop 40, that means auditing Medi-Cal and CalFresh etc. before the election, and requiring recommendations to cut costs by 10% — and the audit costs would be reimbursed from the billionaire tax revenue if it passes. Also the ongoing audits every 4 years of programs receiving money from special taxes enacted on/after Jan 1, 2026 — including SB 125 (Medi-Cal Stability Fund, enacted June 2026). So Prop 41 would immediately impose quadrennial audits of Medi-Cal programs funded by SB 125 and possibly of Prop 35's MCO tax. That's a big deal.

Wait — SB 125: enacted June 2026, imposes MCO tax for 2027-2029 and deposits proceeds into the Medi-Cal Stability Fund. Is that fund excluded from the Gann Limit? The Berkeley memo says "As enacted, the SB 125 tax uses up capacity under the Gann limit" — so it's not excluded; thus Prop 41's Section 3 wouldn't prohibit it, but Section 2's ongoing audits would apply. Hmm, but actually — I need to check whether the Medi-Cal Stability Fund is excluded from the SAL. The memo says the Dept. of Finance Manual of State Funds classifies Fund 3492 (Medi-Cal Stability Fund) as "included". OK.

So Prop 41's practical near-term effects: quadrennial performance audits of Medi-Cal programs (with mandated 10% cost-cut recommendations), audits of Prop 3-funded education programs (if Prop 3 is deemed a new special tax), and the Gann limit lock on future taxes. Plus the risk to Prop 35's MCO tax (which used Art XIII B § 4 to raise the limit — a mechanism Prop 41 prohibits for taxes taking effect on/after Jan 1, 2026; Prop 35's tax takes effect in 2027). That's a serious risk: Prop 35's MCO tax generates roughly $8-19B/yr with federal match; if it "takes effect" after Jan 1, 2026 and is excluded from the SAL via a statutory limit increase, Prop 41 would prohibit the state from imposing/collecting it. That's an enormous unintended consequence — potentially gutting Medi-Cal financing.

Let me verify Prop 35's Gann limit adjustment provision. Search: "Proposition 35 2024 appropriations limit adjustment MCO tax Article XIII B section 4".

Also, let me check the Yes on Prop 41 campaign's response to these concerns — the Mercury News Q&A.

Let me do these two fetches/searches.

## ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST

- ***Paying for Existing Costs in Medi-Cal.*** Some revenue helps pay for existing costs in the Medi-Cal program.

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 41, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026), would require an audit on new or increased special taxes before they appear on the ballot and ongoing audits of programs that receive funding from special taxes. Special taxes may also be subjected to spending limits.
Voting “yes” would mean that the state auditor reviews programs funded by special taxes before they’re on the ballot and on an ongoing basis while opening the possibility that spending limits are attached to the special taxes.

Because of the requirements it imposes on new special taxes, voting “yes” could also mean that Proposition 40 (the “billionaire tax”), even if it gets enough votes, is stopped from becoming law if the courts determine that it conflicts with Prop. 41.
Voting “no” would mean that the state auditor’s role in reviewing government programs stays the same, as would spending limit requirements.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Prohibit Excluding New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Require Special Tax Audits Initiative, favor the increased transparency, oversight and analysis regarding special taxes. More information for the voters.
Generally, opponents don’t like the extra restrictions on how voter-approved tax money is raised and spent and how the programs meant to be funded could be weakened or stalled. They also suggest that Props. 41 and 42 were heavily supported by billionaires in order to defeat Prop. 40.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem is Prop. 41 solving?
State spending is up 79% since 2019. Every year, billions of taxpayer dollars flow into state programs, like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it. Californians deserve better education, health care, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned tax money we pay to the state.
While this is a city wide example, it’s exactly the kind of reason why we need audits and transparent accountability before it’s too late to put programs back on track: Audit: San Jose failed to adequately track $300 million in homelessness spending (https://www.mercurynews.com/2024/04/13/audit-san-jose-failed-to-adequately-track-300-million-in-homelessness-spending/).
Why is this the best solution to the problem?
Prop. 41 requires the independent state auditor to conduct financial and performance audits of the programs to be funded by new special tax measures, with the results posted publicly in the state Voter Information Guide.
This ensures voters have detailed information about the programs they’re being asked to raise taxes to fund.
If taxes are approved, Prop. 41 also requires ongoing public audits of the programs funded by those taxes to evaluate spending, identify waste, fraud or abuse, assess whether they are meeting their intended goals and recommend improvements.
It also requires that all new taxes comply with the state’s voter-approved spending limit — so that excess tax revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
Why is it necessary to audit a tax proposal before it even officially qualifies for the ballot?
Providing pre-ballot information about proposed initiatives is very typical. The Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) and the attorney general are required by state law to provide pre-ballot information on every measure that is filed.
Prop. 41 is actually much narrower — the auditor only commences with an audit once a measure collects 25% of the signatures needed to qualify for the ballot; and it only applies to initiatives that increase taxes.
Prop. 41 requires the independent state auditor to conduct pre-election financial and performance audits of the programs to be funded by proposed new state special taxes. The state auditor’s findings must be shared widely with the public, including in the state’s official Voter Information Guide.
This pre-election audit will give voters clear, unbiased information on the programs a proposed tax would support. These audits are more extensive than any existing information provided to voters. This fills in a critical gap in the information provided to voters. The current initiative analyses from the LAO are required by law to provide only a description of the measure. Alternatively, under Prop. 41 the auditor will also provide voters a performance evaluation of programs funded by new taxes.
If a proposed tax fails to make the ballot, the state’s general fund still has to pay for the audit. Why should taxpayers foot the bill for failed political ideas?
The value to voters in seeing this detailed information about programs before they’re asked to vote far outweighs the marginal cost of conducting the audit and printing it in the Voter Guide.
Again, this is very typical under the status quo. The LAO and the attorney general already have to provide a description and a title and summary for each and every initiative measure — including those that fail — and the General Fund pays for those costs. It is also important to recognize that the extra costs imposed on the General Fund by Prop. 41 are exceedingly small. The LAO found that Prop. 41 would impose only minimal costs upon the General Fund. Further, providing more impartial, expert information to voters when decided to approve higher taxes is money well spent.
This also fails to take into account Prop. 41’s upside. As the LAO noted in the Voter Guide, Prop. 41 would result in taxpayer savings or improved services by implementing the auditor’s recommendations.
Prop. 41 contains conflict provisions stating that if it receives more “yes” votes than a competing tax measure like Prop. 40 (the billionaire wealth tax), then Prop. 40 is nullified entirely. How do proponents respond to claims that Prop. 41 is merely a “poison pill” designed to defeat the wealth tax rather than a stand-alone oversight tool?
California has faced issues with ineffective and inefficient state spending for years: homelessness, state technology programs, EDD are just a few recent examples. Prop. 40 is just the latest proposal that would fuel ineffective spending.
Prop. 40 seeks to raise tens of billions of dollars in new tax revenue, but contains zero transparency, accountability or safeguards to ensure the money is spent as intended. For instance, Prop. 40 contains no safeguards to ensure that billions of dollars don’t flow to health insurance company profits and CEOs under the guise of “saving health care.”
Prop. 40 also exempts itself from the state spending limit, so that the billions in excess tax revenues generated by the measure that would normally flow to taxpayers, schools and the state rainy day fund instead go to the Legislature with no safeguards or accountability. The measure requires the state auditor to find a way to cut an audited program’s costs by 10%. Why mandate a flat 10% cut for every program, regardless of how it operates?
Prop. 41 does not in any way mandate a 10% cut for every program. What Prop. 41 actually says is that the auditor’s report should contain recommendations on how the program could achieve a budgetary savings of 10%. There is no mandate — this is simply one of several factors (at least 10) that the auditor must address when evaluating new spending. The point is to give voters context: For some programs a 10% budget savings may be a good idea and for others it won’t. But right now voters are totally in the dark. Exploring ways to stretch taxpayer dollars farther is always a good idea. But there is no mandate.
The sponsor of Prop. 41 is primarily backed by one billionaire. What makes Prop. 41’s billionaire backer a policy expert capable of devising smart laws for 40 million people?
Prop. 41 is supported by Build Better California, but also has a broad and diverse coalition of organizations and advocacy groups working toward a more transparent California, including small businesses, taxpayers, good government advocates, elected officials, accountants and auditing experts. Specifically, the ballot arguments in support of Prop. 41 were signed by the California Society of Certified Public Accountants, the California Taxpayers Association, a former California State Auditor, the Asian Pacific Islander Chamber of Commerce and former State Controller Steve Westly.
Why should someone in favor of Prop. 40 vote for Prop. 41?
As stated above, state spending is up and billions of dollars are wasted each year in programs that, while well intended, have failed to deliver on the promises made. Prop. 41, by way of the independent State Auditor, will ensure Californians get more accountability, transparency and trackable progress of programs funded by our taxes, so that we stop funding failure and start funding successful outcomes. If both Prop. 40 and Prop. 41 pass and 40 gets more votes, Prop. 41’s provisions will still go into effect to the benefit of voters and taxpayers.
What is the biggest logical error opponents of Prop. 41 make?
Prop. 41’s opponents are all proponents of more taxes and more spending regardless of the accountability, oversight, transparency or trackable metrics needed to help improve the results we get for our tax dollars.
The California State Auditor’s Office is absolutely first-rate and does a fantastic job providing unbiased, nonpartisan, objective information. Getting this type of information to voters, both as part of the Voter Guide and on an ongoing basis (for taxes that are approved), is something that we should have done long ago.
What did we miss? What else should we know?
Voters support the idea of more transparency and accountability. Recent polling shows that 58% support the concept of Prop. 41:
“Q: this measure would require the independent State Auditor to conduct public performance and financial audits of the programs to be funded by proposed new taxes. Knowing this, do you support or oppose this proposal?”

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.mercurynews.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 5:05 PM PST | UPDATED: November 3, 2026 at 4:34 AM PST

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 41, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026), would require an audit on new or increased special taxes before they appear on the ballot and ongoing audits of programs that receive funding from special taxes. Special taxes may also be subjected to spending limits.
Voting “yes” would mean that the state auditor reviews programs funded by special taxes before they’re on the ballot and on an ongoing basis while opening the possibility that spending limits are attached to the special taxes.

How proposed billionaire tax could impact California sports teams (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/proposed-billionaire-tax-could-impact-california-sports-teams-2/)

Another poll finds California billionaires tax losing support (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/29/california-billionaires-tax-prop-40-berkeley-poll-2026/)
Teens work, drive and pay taxes. But should they vote? This California city will soon decide (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/29/teens-work-drive-and-pay-taxes-but-should-they-vote-this-california-city-will-soon-decide-2/)
Because of the requirements it imposes on new special taxes, voting “yes” could also mean that Proposition 40 (the “billionaire tax”), even if it gets enough votes, is stopped from becoming law if the courts determine that it conflicts with Prop. 41.
Voting “no” would mean that the state auditor’s role in reviewing government programs stays the same, as would spending limit requirements.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Prohibit Excluding New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Require Special Tax Audits Initiative, favor the increased transparency, oversight and analysis regarding special taxes. More information for the voters.
Generally, opponents don’t like the extra restrictions on how voter-approved tax money is raised and spent and how the programs meant to be funded could be weakened or stalled. They also suggest that Props. 41 and 42 were heavily supported by billionaires in order to defeat Prop. 40.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/).
What’s the strongest argument against Prop. 41?
Prop. 41 was put on the ballot for one reason — because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share in taxes. This initiative was created to trick voters into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce.
One of Prop. 41’s main funders is Google founder Sergey Brin, whose wealth has doubled to nearly $300 billion. Now he’s spent tens of millions of dollars to fund this sham measure that attempts to cancel out the billionaire tax.
But Prop. 41 isn’t just a scheme, it’s an expensive one. It would require pre-election and ongoing audits of state programs that are funded by new special taxes, costing the state time and money. California already has extensive audit requirements and an independent state auditor who regularly issues reports on state operations.
This initiative isn’t about helping Californians — it’s about billionaires avoiding a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
Don’t voters deserve an unbiased look at how their money will be spent before they vote on a new tax?
California already has an independent state auditor and extensive audit requirements. Prop. 41 goes beyond providing voters with information. It requires a pre-election audit of programs that would receive special-tax revenue, which isn’t only not possible, it interferes with the existing authority of the state auditor.
In addition, any change in audit rules should not undermine the only viable response to $100 billion in federal health care cuts under H.R. 1. Prop. 40 would use funds generated by the billionaire tax to keep hospitals and ERs open, as well as fund health care services that Californians count on like Medicaid and marketplace coverage under the Affordable Care Act. These are all programs that California taxpayers currently fund, and that the Trump administration cut by $100 billion dollars over the next five years. Prop. 40 would backfill those cuts.
What is wrong with forcing government programs to find 10% in cost savings to protect taxpayer dollars?
There’s nothing wrong with finding genuine savings and improving services that California taxpayers support and rely upon. The problem with Prop. 41 is that that is the role of the state auditor, not Sergey Brin.
Prop. 41 doesn’t simply require programs to identify waste. Its audit framework specifically requires recommendations for achieving at least 10% annual budgetary savings and comparisons with analogous private-sector programs.
Those are very different things.
A program may be expensive because the service itself is expensive — not because 10% of its funding is wasted. That’s particularly important for health care, where costs can reflect the escalating costs of prescription drugs, a rapidly aging population, provider shortages and changing federal requirements.
A good government should identify waste, fraud and inefficiency. But that requires evidence, not an arbitrary savings target imposed across fundamentally different programs.
You argue this is a strategy by billionaires to avoid paying taxes. Can you explain exactly how Prop. 41 would block the Prop. 40 wealth tax?
Yes, it hinges on Prop. 41’s Gann Limit provision.
Prop. 41 prohibits collecting state taxes enacted or taking effect after January 1, 2026 if they rely on an exemption or exclusion from the state’s Gann spending limit, which Prop. 40 does.
That’s important because Prop. 40 is a special tax initiative with revenues dedicated to health care services. Without the ability to structure the tax and its spending outside the Gann Limit, the estimated revenue of $100 billion cannot be spent as voters intended.
Prop. 41 creates a new constitutional restriction that directly conflicts with the fiscal structure Prop. 40 requires. Exceptions to the Gann limit are common, and the Gann limit itself, which ties the government to what it spent and prioritized in 1979, is just poor public policy.
If Prop. 41 fails, how else do you suggest California ensure that special tax revenues are being spent efficiently?
California already has mechanisms to do that. The state has extensive audit requirements and an independent state auditor that regularly examines state operations and issues public reports. We should use and strengthen those mechanisms where necessary. The better approach is targeted oversight: audit programs, evaluate outcomes, identify waste or fraud, publish the findings and hold policymakers accountable.
Why should people opposed to Prop. 40 also vote against Prop. 41?
Because Prop. 41 is not limited to Prop. 40. Prop. 41 is likely to endanger other revenue measures, including education funding, taxes connected to Medi-Cal and other health care financing mechanisms.
For instance, Prop. 41 could subject Prop. 3 — the education-funding measure — to its new audit rules. If Prop. 41 receives more votes, it could thereby put Prop. 3’s tax extension at risk of being struck down because of the conflicting language. It could also similarly threaten Medi-Cal taxes and fees that bring the state billions of dollars in federal matching funds.
So someone can oppose Prop. 40 on its merits and still conclude that Prop. 41 goes too far.
If voters don’t like the goals of Prop. 40, they can vote against it. There is no reason to change the state’s constitutional rules for every future special-tax initiative .
Why should people who want the state government to carefully scrutinize how tax dollars are spent still vote against Prop. 41?
Because scrutiny already exists, and Prop. 41 isn’t a carefully written, thoughtful ballot measure. It’s a reckless and dangerous initiative that could undo Prop. 40 and wreak havoc with other taxpayer-funded initiatives that have already been approved by taxpayers. As we’ve shared above, California already has an independent state auditor and extensive audit requirements. If voters are concerned about existing state programs, they can demand better oversight by the auditor and policymakers.
Why shouldn’t programs funded by special taxes face a mandatory check-up every four years to ensure the money isn’t being wasted?
There’s nothing inherently wrong with reviewing programs every four years. The problem is what Prop. 41 requires those reviews to do. They aren’t simply performance check-ups. The audits must examine comparisons with imaginary “private-sector programs” which don’t exist in the case of Medicaid and marketplace insurance coverage.
In addition, Medicaid is one of the most efficient forms of health care coverage (https://healthlaw.org/medicaid-is-even-leaner-as-accountability-improves/) in this country, and 1 in 5 of Californians count on it for their health care. This includes children, people with disabilities, seniors and many veterans.
While federal health care programs can always be strengthened and improved, the most urgent issue facing Californians right now is ensuring billionaires pay their fair share to keep local hospitals and ERs open and health care affordable for millions of working people.
What is the biggest logical error proponents of Prop. 41 make?
They are counting on the fact that California voters won’t see through their poison pill ballot measure, which we believe they will. Prop. 41 was put on the ballot for one reason — because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. This initiative was created to trick voters into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce.
This initiative isn’t about helping California taxpayers — it’s about defeating one specific tax that billionaires want to avoid, because they would rather millions of working people lose health care than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
What did we miss? What else should we know?
In short, Prop. 41 would insert constitutional barriers in the way of future voters trying to fund health care, education and other public priorities just because Sergy Brin doesn’t want to pay a modest 5% tax on his vast wealth. Instead, he’d like to shift the cost of keeping hospitals, ERs and clinics open onto ordinary taxpayers, who already pay higher effective tax rates than billionaires do.
Prop. 41 is deceptive, dangerous, deeply unfair, and we believe California voters will vote “no” on this measure.

Locking all new taxes into it means a voter-approved tax may not be spendable for its purpose when the state hits the cap — the opposite of "accountability." LWV opposed Gann in 1979 for exactly this reason.

But you can simply vote No on Prop 40 directly. The problem is Prop 41 has permanent structural consequences far beyond Prop 40 — it's a constitutional amendment (can't be repealed by the Legislature) that locks in a 1979-era spending cap for all future taxes and creates an audit regime, and it may jeopardize existing Medi-Cal financing. And the risk is asymmetric: Prop 40's fate is uncertain, while Prop 41's harms are permanent and broad.

Also, importantly, Prop 41 has an internal inconsistency: two sections numbered "SEC. 5" (one in Article XXIV about applicability, one about conflicting measures). Minor drafting sloppiness but indicative.

Additionally, the nullification mechanism: Prop 41 says if it gets more votes, "all the provisions of the other measure shall be null and void" — that's a total nullification, even of provisions that don't conflict (e.g., Prop 3's rate extension, Prop 40's healthcare funding). That's an extraordinary voter-disenfranchising device.

So my recommendation: NO.

**No.**

**What Prop 41 actually does (Nov. 3, 2026 ballot):** It adds Article XXIV to the state Constitution to (1) require the State Auditor to run pre‑election performance/financial audits of programs that would be funded by any initiative special tax (triggered at 25% of signatures), with a mandate to recommend ≥10% annual cost cuts and comparisons to "analogous programs in the nongovernment sector," printed in the Voter Guide right after the LAO's impartial analysis; (2) require audits every four years of programs funded by special taxes enacted on/after Jan. 1, 2026; and (3) bar the state from imposing, collecting, or enforcing **any** tax enacted or taking effect on/after Jan. 1, 2026 that is excluded from the Gann Limit — including via a statutory appropriations-limit increase under Art. XIII B §4.

**Why I'm voting no:**

- **It's a concealed nullification device.** Its conflict clause voids *all* provisions of any same-ballot measure containing a Gann-excluded tax if Prop 41 gets more "yes" votes — killing Prop 40 even if a majority approves it, and potentially Prop 3 (the education millionaire's tax, which carries different audit rules). The title, summary, and yes-argument never mention this. If you oppose the billionaire tax, you can vote no on Prop 40 directly; you don't need to permanently rewrite the Constitution to do it.
- **Serious, well-documented collateral damage.** Because §4(b)(2) bans appropriations-limit increases by statute, tax-law scholars (Galle/Gamage/Shanske, Aug. 2026 memo) and the nonpartisan California Budget & Policy Center warn Prop 41 could jeopardize the MCO tax, Hospital Quality Assurance Fee, and SNF fee — mechanisms that draw down roughly $8+ billion/yr in federal Medi-Cal matching funds — plus SB 125's Medi-Cal Stability Fund (enacted June 2026). It also hands opponents of *any* future tax initiative a new single-subject litigation weapon, since escaping Prop 41 would require bundling a constitutional override with a tax.
- **The Gann lock is bad policy, not accountability.** The 1979 cap grows only with population + inflation. Voters could approve a dedicated tax and find the state legally unable to spend it on the intended purpose when it's near the cap — excess goes to rebates/schools instead. The League of Women Voters opposed Gann in 1979 for this inflexibility and opposes Prop 41; SPUR, CA Budget & Policy Center, CA Democratic Party, and the SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee, LA Times, and Mercury News editorial boards all say no. (Notably, outlets that also oppose Prop 40 still say no on 41 — calling it a "cynical poison pill.")
- **The audits are redundant and tilted.** California already has an independent State Auditor with high-risk, legislative-request, and whistleblower audit authority; Prop 30/3 revenues are already audited. The new regime is prescriptive (arbitrary 10% savings target, private-sector benchmarking), costs the General Fund when initiatives fail, and can require auditing programs that don't yet exist — a chilling tax on the citizen initiative itself.
- **Money and motive:** ~$58M to the yes committee, nearly all from Building a Better California ($102M from Sergey Brin alone; $186M across Props 41/42), which also spent ~$118M against Prop 40.

The one legitimate idea here — more performance auditing before new taxes — is already achievable through the State Auditor and Legislature, without a permanent constitutional cap-lock, without a hidden poison pill, and without risking billions in federal health funding.
